newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Lebanon guerrilla rockets batter Israel, one hurt.
newsitem.headline: Lebanon guerrilla rockets batter Israel, one hurt.

text.p: Dozens of Katyusha rockets fired from Lebanon slammed into northern Israel early on Tuesday, injuring at least one civilian and causing some damage, witnesses said.
The attack just after 7 a.m. (0400 GMT) occurred a day after violence in Lebanon, some of it involving pro-Israeli militia, killed at least nine civilians.

Israeli troops, bracing for another possible rocket barrage, ordered residents of the main border town of Kiryat Shmona into shelters about 45 minutes after the Katyushas fell. Hospitals went on emergency alert.
A second attack on western Galilee around 8 a.m. caused no injuries or damage, residents said.

"I awoke at 6:30 in the morning. At 7 we heard on the news on the television that it's quiet, everything's OK, and then precisely three or four minutes later there was a barrage of Katyushas, at least 20 or 30 -- a quantity I've never heard before," a resident named Gavriel told Israeli army radio.
The wounded man, Ehud Molad, bleeding from chest wounds, told reporters he was driving to work when the Katyushas fell.
In Lebanon, pro-Israeli militia sources said a 65-year-old woman was also wounded. But Israeli ambulance workers said Molad, who was lightly injured, was the only Israeli wounded.

Israeli television stations showed pictures of a house that took a direct hit in Kiryat Shmona. Witnesses said rockets fell all across the north of Israel -- both in western Galilee and what is known as the Galilee Panhandle.

In Beirut, a spokesman for Hizbollah, the Iranian-backed "Party of God," said he had no immediate information about the attacks although pro-Israeli militia sources said Hizbollah was responsible for them.

Hizbollah has been trying to oust Israeli troops and militiamen of the Israeli-backed South Lebanon Army militia from a 15-km (nine-mile) deep border zone set up inside Lebanon with the declared aim of preventing guerrilla attacks on northern Israel.

Asked what should be done next, Israel's coordinator of policy in Lebanon, Uri Lubrani, told Israel Radio: "At the moment -- go into the shelters and listen to the orders of the northern command. At the political level -- to search in every way to calm the situation."

Israel distanced itself from the fighting on Monday in which Lebanese militiamen led by pro-Israeli commander Antoine Lahd killed six civilians and wounded 36, many seriously, in shelling of the southern port of Sidon.
Israel strongly denied firing those shells and blamed the incident on forces serving under Lahd around the Jezzine area outside the occupation zone patrolled by Israel and Lahd's South Lebanon Army.

Israeli military officials said Lahd's men were apparently avenging the deaths of three youths killed by a roadside bomb in the Jezzine area earlier on Monday. The army accused Hizbollah of carrying out that attack.
